title: Laws for Life in the Land
overview: Right after the people are told they will wander for forty years, the LORD gives laws that assume their children will still reach the promised land, covering offerings, mistakes, defiance and remembering.

parts.label: Grain and wine with sacrifices (vv. 1-12)
parts.note: Opening with "after you enter the land" quietly promises that the next generation will get there, despite the judgment in the previous chapter. Every animal offering was to come with flour, olive oil and wine, like a full meal, and the amounts grew with the size of the animal.

parts.label: One rule for everyone (vv. 13-16)
parts.note: Foreigners living among Israel who worshiped the LORD followed exactly the same rules as those born Israelite. When it came to worship, being born Israelite gave no one an advantage before God.

parts.label: The first of the dough (vv. 17-21)
parts.note: Once they farmed their own land instead of eating manna, the food God provided in the desert, they were to give the first loaf from their dough to God, and it went to the priests. It was a way of saying that their daily bread still came from God.

parts.label: Mistakes versus defiance (vv. 22-31)
parts.note: Wrongs done by accident, whether by the whole nation or one person, could be forgiven through set offerings. A wrong done openly and on purpose, in defiance of God, had no offering, and the person was "cut off", which scholars think meant either being expelled or dying by God's hand.

parts.label: The man gathering wood (vv. 32-36)
parts.note: A man was caught gathering wood on the Sabbath, the weekly day of rest, and was held until God gave a ruling, after which the community stoned him. It is a harsh story, most likely placed here as an example of open defiance, and the text offers no softening explanation.

parts.label: Tassels as reminders (vv. 37-41)
parts.note: Israelites were to wear tassels with a blue cord on the corners of their clothes, so that seeing them would remind them of God's commands instead of following every impulse. Many Jewish people still wear these tassels today.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the defiant sin of verses 30 and 31 describes a sin that can never be forgiven or a hardened stance that a person can still turn away from.
think: Where do you draw the line between an honest mistake and a deliberate wrong, and should that line change how a wrong is treated?
